chunks.evidence: 'Which of these are actually realised is also influenced by as yet insufficiently understood processes of nucleation and crystal growth.'

chunks.statement: The blind test protocol gives participants only 2D molecular diagrams and requires three ranked candidate structures per target, with the true structure withheld until submission.
chunks.scope: CCDC CSP blind test format 2004
chunks.evidence: 'the participants were given molecular diagrams of three molecules and asked to submit three predictions for the most likely crystal structure of each.'

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0 the CSP2004 lessons are directly on the critical path: the two hardest failure modes flagged here, Z'>1 packings and conformational flexibility, are exactly the frontiers modern GA-MCSP still pushes on. The Z'=2 surprise on a 'simple' rigid molecule is a caution that Genarris generation and GA crossover/mutation operators must sample larger asymmetric units and richer symmetry rather than assuming Z'=1, and that niching must maintain diversity across Z' families so a correct multi-molecule minimum is not crowded out. The abstract's core message that energy models must describe conformation and packing simultaneously with high accuracy is precisely the case for dispersion-inclusive DFT (PBE0+MBD) reranking and for conformer-energy-aware MLIPs (MACE-OFF, AIMNet2, UMA); a GA that optimizes an inaccurate surface will converge confidently to the wrong crystal. Finally, the nucleation/growth caveat reminds you that even flawless finite-temperature free-energy ranking only predicts what is thermodynamically accessible, not what nature selects, so blind-test scoring should reward populating the low-energy landscape, not just top-1 hits.

records.title: Significant progress in predicting the crystal structures of small organic molecules – a report on the fourth blind test
records.core_idea: The fourth blind test of crystal structure prediction (2009) evaluated the state of computational CSP by challenging 14 groups to predict four target crystal structures (three single-component, one 1:1 cocrystal) from molecular diagrams alone. It demonstrated a dramatic improvement over previous blind tests, with 13 successful predictions and at least two groups getting each target right.
records.innovation: First blind test to show a marked jump in success rates, including one group correctly predicting all four targets as first-ranked choices; also introduced a cocrystal (1:1) as a target, extending CSP beyond single-component systems.

chunks.statement: In the fourth blind test, 14 groups tackled four targets; there were 13 successful predictions overall, with at least two groups correctly predicting each of the four target structures.
chunks.scope: Small, fairly rigid organic molecules; three single-component crystals and one 1:1 cocrystal; three allowed predictions per target.
chunks.evidence: '14 research groups which took part... four target systems: three single-component crystal structures and a 1:1 cocrystal... in total, there were 13 successful predictions and, for each of the four targets, at least two groups correctly predicted the observed crystal structure.'

chunks.statement: CSP success rates improved dramatically between the third and fourth blind tests, attributed to important improvements in modelling (generation and ranking) methods.
chunks.scope: Small, fairly rigid organic molecules as of 2009.
chunks.evidence: 'The results demonstrate a dramatic improvement in rates of success over previous blind tests... The results reflect important improvements in modelling methods.'

chunks.statement: For small and fairly rigid molecules, CSP calculations are reliable enough to constructively help understand crystallization and polymorphism; results should not be extrapolated to larger or more flexible molecules.
chunks.scope: Small, fairly rigid organic molecules only, as demonstrated in the 2009 blind test.
chunks.evidence: 'at least for the small and fairly rigid types of molecules included in this blind test, such calculations can be constructively applied to help understand crystallization and polymorphism.'

chunks.statement: Top-ranked CSP success can come at considerable computational expense; getting the observed structure as the first ranked choice may require methods too costly for routine application.
chunks.scope: Blind test conditions; the one group that correctly ranked all four targets first.
chunks.evidence: 'one participating group who correctly predicted all four crystal structures as their first ranked choice, albeit at a considerable computational expense.'

chunks.statement: The blind test protocol gives participants only molecular diagrams, withholds the experimentally determined (unpublished) structures via an independent referee, and allows three ranked predictions per target - a two-stage generate-then-rank challenge.
chunks.scope: CSP blind test methodology, fourth test (2009).
chunks.evidence: 'Participants were challenged to predict the crystal structures... given only their molecular diagrams, while the recently determined but as-yet unpublished crystal structures were withheld by an independent referee. Three predictions were allowed for each system.'

records.synthesis:
For GAtor 2.0, this blind test is a historical benchmark showing that even by 2009 the generate-then-rank paradigm worked well for small rigid Z'=1 molecules - which is exactly why modern GA-CSP effort has shifted toward the hard cases (flexible molecules, Z'>1, cocrystals, finite-temperature effects). The single cocrystal target foreshadowed multi-component CSP where your niching and structure generation (Genarris) must handle stoichiometric composition and packing space that is far larger. The lesson that first-rank success came 'at considerable computational expense' is precisely the motivation for MLIP surrogates (MACE-OFF, AIMNet2, UMA) plus dispersion-inclusive DFT (PBE0+MBD) reranking: you want the accuracy that ranks the true structure at the top without the exhaustive cost. Treat the 'small and rigid' caveat as a boundary marker - GA operators, niching, and finite-temperature free-energy ranking are the tools for pushing beyond where 2009 methods succeeded.

Confidence: low - digest is from abstract/metadata only; specific target identities, per-method energies, and ranking details are not available.

records.title: Accurate Molecular Van Der Waals Interactions from Ground-State Electron Density and Free-Atom Reference Data
records.core_idea: This paper introduces the TS (Tkatchenko-Scheffler) van der Waals method: a parameter-free way to compute pairwise C6 dispersion coefficients and vdW radii for atoms in molecules by rescaling accurate free-atom reference values (Chu-Dalgarno) using the ratio of the atom's Hirshfeld-partitioned effective volume in the molecule to its free-atom volume. Effective atomic polarizabilities, and hence C6 coefficients, thus respond automatically to the local bonding environment from the ground-state electron density.
records.innovation: Prior density-based C6 schemes had 15-20% average errors (up to 40-60%) because DFT polarizabilities are grossly overestimated; earlier C6/R6 corrections (Grimme) fit parameters empirically to experimental C6 or post-HF binding energies. TS instead uses the electron density only to compute the RELATIVE polarizability (effective/free-atom volume ratio), keeping absolute accuracy from free-atom references, cutting the C6 error to 5.5% and making the coefficients depend explicitly on hybridization/bonding without fitting.

chunks.statement: The TS method reproduces intermolecular C6 coefficients with a mean absolute relative error of 5.5% (4.5% if H2 is excluded) against 1225 experimental DOSD-derived pairs, a factor of 2-3 better than prior ground-state-density C6 methods (which had 15-20% average, 40-60% max errors).
chunks.scope: 8 atoms and 42 small-to-medium organic/inorganic molecules (up to C8H18), Z'=1 gas-phase geometries
chunks.evidence: 'mean absolute error in the C6 coefficients is 5.5%... for 1225 intermolecular pairs'; 'if the H2 molecule is excluded... the MARE drops down to 4.5%'; existing methods errors '15%-20% on average and maximum deviation of 40%-60%'

chunks.statement: Effective atomic C6 coefficients depend strongly on an atom's bonding environment; using the ground-state density to rescale free-atom polarizabilities automatically captures hybridization state and charge polarization (e.g. carbon C6 ranges 24-33, matching sp3-methane vs sp2-benzene expectations).
chunks.scope: Light main-group atoms (C, N, O, H, Si, S, Cl, F) in molecules and simple solids
chunks.evidence: atom-in-molecule C6 for C ranges 24.1-33.0 vs free-atom 46.6, matching Wu-Yang 22.1-29.8; graphene C=33.0 (near benzene sp2 30.3), diamond C=38.6 vs methane sp3 24.1

chunks.statement: Computing C6 from the RATIO of effective to free-atom Hirshfeld volumes makes the result nearly independent of the exchange-correlation functional, because density differences between functionals cancel in the ratio.
chunks.scope: LDA, PBE, BLYP tested on the molecular database
chunks.evidence: MARE in C6 between LDA and PBE is 1.4% (max 3.8%), BLYP vs PBE 0.68% (max 2.1%); 'difference in the electron density between xc functionals is compensated when computing the ratio'

chunks.statement: The assumption that the polarizability-to-volume proportionality constant is unchanged from free atom to atom-in-molecule (set to unity) is excellent for most molecules but breaks down for very small systems, especially H2.
chunks.scope: Small molecules; H2 is the worst case
chunks.evidence: 'this approximation breaks down only for the smallest H2 molecule, with deviation of 44%'; already for N2 and CO2 error < 10%

chunks.statement: Pairwise C6/R6 summation neglects nonadditive many-body/higher-order effects and can fail qualitatively for metallic low-dimensional systems; the atoms-in-molecules concept itself breaks where atomic partitioning is ill-defined.
chunks.scope: Metallic low-dimensional systems and cases where atoms-in-molecules cannot be applied
chunks.evidence: 'a pairwise summation of C6R6 interactions can fail qualitatively for metallic low-dimensional systems due to nonadditive higher-order effects'

chunks.statement: To couple the long-range dispersion to DFT one needs a short-range damping function with vdW radii scaled by the effective volume; the recommended Fermi damping steepness d=20 works for 12<d<45 (small d corrupts covalent bonds, large d gives kinked curves), leaving one system-specific scaling parameter sR (0.94 for PBE) fit to the S22 CCSD(T) benchmark.
chunks.scope: CNOH light elements; PBE functional benchmarked on S22 dimers (23 meV CH4 to 0.9 eV uracil)
chunks.evidence: 'choice of d=20 turned out to satisfy both constraints'; 'sR... single empirical parameter'; 'sR coefficient for PBE is 0.94'

chunks.statement: TS+PBE gives a mean absolute error of 13 meV on the S22 benchmark (20/13/6 meV for H-bonded/vdW/mixed), versus 20 meV (29/20/9) for empirical C6+vdW-radii schemes; the improvement in H-bonded systems comes from larger effective vdW radii for atoms in hydrogen bonds.
chunks.scope: S22 database of 22 noncovalent dimers, PBE functional
chunks.evidence: 'MAE of our approach on the S22 database is 13 meV (20, 13, and 6 meV...)... compared to 20 meV (29, 20, and 9 meV) when using empirical C6 coefficients'

chunks.statement: Hydrogen bonding measurably redistributes polarizability: the donor H and donor O become more polarizable while the acceptor O and its H become less polarizable, and this is a purely electronic effect visible at fixed geometry.
chunks.scope: Water dimer as illustrative case
chunks.evidence: 'hydrogen involved in the hydrogen bond becomes significantly more polarizable along with the donor oxygen... acceptor oxygen becomes less polarizable'; 'change in the C6 coefficients is a purely electronic effect' at fixed geometry

records.synthesis: TS is the dispersion foundation on which GAtor's lattice-energy ranking (PBE0+MBD, whose MBD is the many-body successor to this pairwise TS) is built, so understanding its logic is directly load-bearing for CSP ranking decisions. Two lessons matter most for MCSP: (1) the density-ratio construction means C6 coefficients adapt to each polymorph's local bonding/H-bonding environment automatically - so ranking near-degenerate polymorphs that differ mainly in H-bond networks genuinely benefits from environment-dependent dispersion rather than fixed atomic C6, which is exactly the regime where polymorph energies sit within a few kJ/mol. (2) The explicit warning that pairwise C6/R6 misses nonadditive many-body screening is the reason GAtor should prefer MBD (or MBD-derived methods) over plain TS/D2-style corrections for dense, extended crystals where collective response is strong; this also flags that MLIP dispersion (MACE-OFF, AIMNet2) must be checked for whether it captures beyond-pairwise effects. The near functional-independence of the volume ratio is reassuring for cross-functional consistency, but the H2/small-molecule breakdown and the single empirical sR per functional are reminders that damping/short-range coupling still carries system-specific risk when comparing polymorphs at their true equilibrium contact distances.

records.title: Accurate and Efficient Method for Many-Body van der Waals Interactions
records.core_idea: The paper introduces the many-body dispersion (MBD) method: it augments the Tkatchenko-Scheffler atom-in-molecule vdW scheme with a classical self-consistent screening (SCS) equation to capture long-range electrostatic (de)polarization, then computes the fully nonadditive vdW energy to infinite order via coupled quantum harmonic oscillators (CFDM). Screening and many-body effects are shown to matter even for small molecules and become crucial for biomolecule conformers and molecular crystals.
records.innovation: Prior vdW corrections neglected long-range electrostatic screening and truncated many-body effects at pairwise (or three-body Axilrod-Teller). This work adds SCS screening to effective atomic polarizabilities and solves a coupled-oscillator Hamiltonian for the vdW energy to infinite order in the dipole approximation, all at negligible computational cost, with a single physically motivated range-separation parameter per functional.

chunks.statement: Pairwise-additive dispersion overestimates polarizability and C6 in large/extended systems because it ignores long-range electrostatic screening (depolarization) from distant fluctuating dipoles; self-consistent screening corrects this.
chunks.scope: Finite-gap molecules, hydrogen-saturated Si clusters, and bulk Si
chunks.evidence: TS-vdW C6 error grows with cluster size to 27% for Si172H120 and 68% overestimation for Si bulk C6; adding SCS gives depolarization reducing bulk error to just 8%.

chunks.statement: Many-body/screening corrections shift molecular-crystal cohesive energies by well over 100 meV/molecule, turning a large overbinding into near-experimental agreement.
chunks.scope: Benzene molecular crystal at experimental geometry, PBE-based
chunks.evidence: PBE+TS-vdW gives 690 meV/molecule vs experiment 518-560 meV/molecule; PBE+MBD yields 565 meV/molecule.

chunks.statement: MBD substantially improves intermolecular binding energies over pairwise TS-vdW on standard benchmarks.
chunks.scope: S22 intermolecular database, binding energies 23-895 meV, vs CCSD(T) basis-set limit
chunks.evidence: MARE decreased from 9.2% (PBE+TS-vdW) to 5.4% (PBE+MBD); vdW-bound subset MARE reduced by ~10%.

chunks.statement: Many-body dispersion can flip conformational rankings: pairwise dispersion may predict the wrong most-stable conformer.
chunks.scope: 27 conformers of alanine tetrapeptide (Ace-Ala3-NMe), PBE0-based, vs CCSD(T)
chunks.evidence: PBE0+TS-vdW MAE 0.52 kcal/mol but predicts wrong most-stable conformer and wrong hierarchy; PBE0+MBD MAE 0.29 kcal/mol, correct most-stable conformer; differences reach ~1 kcal/mol.

chunks.statement: The screened many-body vdW energy is obtained as the difference of zero-point energies between coupled and uncoupled oscillators, and this coupled-oscillator model can be derived as an approximation to the exact ACFDT correlation energy.
chunks.scope: Systems where the polarizability is even in frequency with simple poles on/below the real axis
chunks.evidence: EvdW = (1/2)sum sqrt(lambda_p) - (3/2)sum omega_p; derivable from ACFDT since correlation energy equals difference of zero-point energies under those pole conditions.

chunks.statement: Anisotropy in molecular polarizability comes largely from long-range dipole field screening, not just atomic partitioning; screening becomes less important for integrated C6 because response grows isotropic at high imaginary frequency.
chunks.scope: 17 small molecules H2 to cyclohexane, N2 example
chunks.evidence: TS-vdW fractional anisotropy error 80%, reduced to 23% with SCS; TS-vdW C6 error (5.5%) far better than static polarizability error (~12%) because response isotropizes at large i-omega.

chunks.statement: Couple the many-body dispersion to the DFT functional through a range-separated (damped) Coulomb potential rather than ad hoc pairwise damping functions, fitting one beta parameter per functional.
chunks.scope: DFA+MBD with GGA/hybrid functionals; beta>=2 so potential vanishes at zero distance
chunks.evidence: beta=2.56 for PBE, 2.53 for PBE0, fit to S22; vdW radius R_vdW_p = (alpha_SCS/alpha_free)^(1/3) R_vdW,free from coupled-cluster free-atom reference.

chunks.statement: MBD workflow: partition density into atoms (Hirshfeld), build TS effective atomic polarizabilities, solve SCS for screened static polarizability and characteristic frequency, then diagonalize the 3Nx3N coupled-oscillator matrix for the vdW energy.
chunks.scope: Finite-gap molecules and condensed matter, atoms modeled as Gaussian QHOs
chunks.evidence: SCS omega defined to reproduce C6_SCS from Casimir-Polder integral; MBD energy for 1000 atoms takes ~3 min on a single processor (DFT not included).

chunks.statement: Truncating many-body vdW at three-body Axilrod-Teller can give even the wrong sign for the many-body vdW energy.
chunks.scope: General many-body dispersion beyond pairwise
chunks.evidence: Stated that three-body Axilrod-Teller treatment 'might even give the wrong sign for the many-body vdW energy'.

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0, this is the physics case for why PBE0+MBD (rather than pairwise TS-vdW or D3) is the right final ranking method: molecular crystals are exactly the extended, densely-packed systems where long-range depolarization suppresses overbinding by >100 meV/molecule and where many-body terms can reorder near-degenerate polymorphs whose energy differences are only a few kJ/mol. The conformer result is directly relevant to Z'>1 and flexible molecules where GA must resolve conformational hierarchies -- pairwise dispersion can pick the wrong most-stable structure. Practically, MBD's negligible cost (~3 min/1000 atoms) means it is affordable for large candidate pools, and the screened, anisotropic polarizabilities it produces are also a physically grounded basis for dispersion-aware descriptors used in de-duplication and niching.

records.title: Role of Dispersion Interactions in the Polymorphism and Entropic Stabilization of the Aspirin Crystal
records.core_idea: Aspirin forms I and II are degenerate in lattice energy (within ~0.1 kJ/mol), so lattice-energy ranking cannot explain why form I dominates. Including many-body dispersion (MBD) in both the lattice energy AND the phonons reveals an entropic, finite-temperature mechanism: MBD softens low-frequency phonons in form I (via plasmon-phonon coupling), raising its vibrational entropy and making it thermodynamically more stable at room temperature by ~2.56 kJ/mol.
records.innovation: First demonstration that many-body vdW interactions affect not just lattice energies but lattice vibrations, uncovering a coupling between collective electronic (plasmon) fluctuations and low-frequency phonons that shifts frequencies down. Prior work treated the polymorphs as degenerate and invoked kinetics; this provides a thermodynamic, entropy-driven explanation and also rules out mechanical instability of form II.

chunks.statement: The two observed aspirin polymorphs are essentially degenerate in lattice energy, with 0 K differences of order 0.1 kJ/mol; MBD gives +0.04 kJ/mol, TS gives -0.18 kJ/mol, and PBE0+MBD differs from PBE+MBD by only 0.1 kJ/mol.
chunks.scope: Aspirin forms I and II, static 0 K DFT lattice energies with pairwise (TS) and many-body (MBD) dispersion
chunks.evidence: Table I: PBE+TS -0.18, PBE+MBD 0.04 kJ/mol; text: 'very small energy differences of the order of 0.1 kJ/mol... essentially degenerate'; 'PBE0+MBD... differing by only 0.1 kJ/mol'

chunks.statement: Zero-point energy corrections to the polymorph energy difference are small (0.2-0.3 kJ/mol, consistent with a prior 0.4 kJ/mol), but the finite-temperature vibrational free-energy contribution at 298 K is large and method-dependent: PBE+MBD gives a +2.56 kJ/mol preference for form I while PBE+TS gives a -0.68 kJ/mol preference for form II.
chunks.scope: Aspirin forms I/II, harmonic free energies at 298 K, PBE+TS vs PBE+MBD
chunks.evidence: Table I: PBE+MBD+Fvib(298 K) 2.56, PBE+TS+Fvib(298 K) -0.68 kJ/mol; ZPE 0.2-0.3 kJ/mol

chunks.statement: Many-body dispersion couples collective electronic (plasmon-like) excitations to lattice phonons: although plasmon energies (~8 eV) are ~1000x larger than phonon energies (tens of meV), the change in vdW energy along phonon motions is several meV, enough to renormalize and soften low-frequency phonons. Geometry-dependent static polarizability drives this renormalization while atomic reference frequencies stay fixed.
chunks.scope: Molecular crystals with soft low-frequency lattice/librational modes; demonstrated for aspirin via the MBD Hamiltonian
chunks.evidence: MBD energy Eq (2); 'change of the vdW energy associated to characteristic phonon motions... on the order of several meV, making plasmon-phonon coupling possible'; MBD introduces four modes at 28-34 cm-1 absent in pure PBE

chunks.statement: Lower-frequency phonon modes are more easily thermally populated, so a polymorph with softer lattice vibrations has higher vibrational entropy and lower free energy. Entropic stabilization can flip a ranking that lattice energy alone leaves ambiguous.
chunks.scope: Nearly lattice-energy-degenerate polymorphs at finite temperature (harmonic free energy)
chunks.evidence: 'lower-frequency vibrations of form I are more easily thermally populated, increasing its entropy and ultimately leading to a lower free energy'

chunks.statement: When candidate polymorphs are near-degenerate in lattice energy, compute finite-temperature free energies including phonons treated with the same dispersion model used for the energy; pairwise vs many-body dispersion can give qualitatively opposite rankings, so the vibrational treatment must be dispersion-consistent.
chunks.scope: Ranking near-degenerate molecular crystal polymorphs where thermal effects may dominate
chunks.evidence: PBE+TS predicts form II stable, PBE+MBD predicts form I stable by 2.56 kJ/mol; 'majority of the PBE+MBD free-energy difference arises from thermal vibrational contributions'

chunks.statement: Pairwise dispersion (TS) can misplace internal degrees of freedom that couple to phonons: TS gave a methyl torsion of 47.1 deg while MBD gave 60.1 deg, matching the 20 K neutron value of 58.2 deg. Wrong geometry propagates into wrong vibrational spectra and thus wrong free-energy rankings.
chunks.scope: Molecular crystals with flexible/rotatable groups (methyl torsions) sensitive to dispersion model
chunks.evidence: PBE+TS torsion 47.1 deg vs PBE+MBD 60.1 deg vs neutron 58.2 deg at 20 K; similar >10 deg difference for form II

chunks.statement: Directional elastic measurements can mislead about relative stability: nanoindentation suggested form II is 'considerably softer' and mechanically unstable, but full Young's-modulus analysis showed form II is only softer along some directions and much stiffer in the e1e3 plane (transverse to its stronger hydrogen bonds), which the experiments never probed. Both forms satisfy the Born stability criterion.
chunks.scope: Elastic/mechanical stability assessment of molecular crystal polymorphs
chunks.evidence: Fig 4; 'nanoindentation experiments did not probe along this hard direction'; lambda_min = 2.60 GPa (form I), 1.86 GPa (form II), both positive; exp lambda_min 2.40 GPa at 300 K

chunks.statement: Dispersion treatment strongly affects computed elastic moduli: MBD reduces bulk modulus by over 20% vs TS (form I bulk 12.40 -> 9.58 GPa; exp 7.77 GPa), and even flips the qualitative ordering of the shear modulus (TS: form I 5.08 > form II 4.33; MBD: form I 4.00 < form II 4.67 GPa).
chunks.scope: Aspirin forms I/II elastic constants, PBE+TS vs PBE+MBD vs 300 K experiment
chunks.evidence: Table II: bulk moduli and shear moduli listed; 'MBD reduces the bulk modulus by over 20% compared to TS'

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0 this is a cautionary tale about the endpoint of any GA-MCSP pipeline: after the GA converges on a pool of low-energy structures ranked by dispersion-inclusive DFT (PBE0+MBD), near-degenerate survivors (which aspirin-like landscapes will always produce) cannot be discriminated by lattice energy at all. The paper shows the discriminating physics is vibrational entropy, and critically that the SAME dispersion model must be used for the phonons, not just the static energy - a pairwise vs many-body choice can invert the winner. Practically: (1) treat sub-~2 kJ/mol energy gaps in the final ranking as unresolved without free energies; (2) budget for harmonic (or quasi-harmonic) phonon calculations on the top candidates; (3) beware that MLIPs (MACE-OFF, AIMNet2, UMA) used for cheap relaxation/ranking may not capture the plasmon-phonon softening or the correct methyl-torsion geometry that MBD does, so validate soft-mode frequencies and flexible-group torsions before trusting entropy-driven rankings. The methyl-torsion error also flags that flexible-molecule conformers coupled to lattice modes are a place where cheaper dispersion/energy models silently corrupt downstream vibrational thermodynamics.

records.title: Towards crystal structure prediction of complex organic compounds – a report on the fifth blind test
records.core_idea: The fifth CSP blind test (CSP2010) evaluated diverse computational methods against six organic targets spanning rigid molecules, a semi-flexible molecule, a 1:1 salt, a large flexible molecule, and a polymorphic hydrate. At least one group succeeded on every target, and dispersion-corrected DFT emerged as a reliable route for ranking the smaller systems.
records.innovation: Introduced two new, harder target categories not present in prior blind tests: a large, highly flexible molecule and a multi-polymorph hydrate; and provided the first strong evidence that DFT-D can reliably predict small-molecule crystal structures.

chunks.statement: Dispersion-corrected DFT (DFT-D) can reliably predict the crystal structures of small rigid organic molecules, marking a maturation of lattice-energy ranking methods.
chunks.scope: Small rigid and semi-flexible organic molecules, Z'=1-scale targets in CSP2010
chunks.evidence: Abstract: 'there is now evidence that methodologies such as dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT-D) are able to reliably do so' for the three smallest molecules

chunks.statement: Every target in CSP2010 (six molecules across five categories) had at least one successful blind prediction, and the large flexible molecule was correctly ranked first by two groups.
chunks.scope: Six CSP2010 organic targets; each group submitted three predictions per attempted target
chunks.evidence: Abstract: 'There was at least one successful prediction for each target, and two groups were able to successfully predict the structure of the large flexible molecule as their first place submission'

chunks.statement: Success rates can drop for the smallest, seemingly easiest molecules even as harder targets are solved, so fewer groups succeeding is not simple evidence of harder targets.
chunks.scope: CSP2010 vs CSP2007 comparison of the three smallest molecules
chunks.evidence: Abstract: 'not as many groups successfully predicted the structures of the three smallest molecules as in CSP2007'

chunks.statement: Treat molecular flexibility, salts, and hydrates/solvates as distinct difficulty tiers requiring dedicated handling beyond rigid-molecule protocols.
chunks.scope: CSP target categories: rigid, semi-flexible, 1:1 salt, large flexible, polymorphic hydrate
chunks.evidence: Abstract distinguishes 'two rigid molecules, one semi-flexible molecule and a 1:1 salt' from 'new challenging categories - a larger, much more flexible molecule and a hydrate with more than one polymorph'

chunks.statement: The blind-test protocol has groups submit a limited number of ranked predictions (three per target) using their own end-to-end generation-plus-ranking methodologies, enabling head-to-head method comparison.
chunks.scope: CSP2010 collaborative blind test organized at CCDC
chunks.evidence: Abstract: 'A range of methodologies was used by the participating groups... Each group submitted three predictions for each target it attempted'

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0, CSP2010 is the historical inflection point where dispersion-inclusive DFT (the ancestor of your PBE0+MBD ranking stage) proved trustworthy for small rigid organics -- validating the two-stage 'generate broadly, re-rank with dispersion-DFT' philosophy your GA embodies. The lesson that flexible molecules, salts, and hydrates form separate difficulty tiers maps directly onto why GAtor invests in conformer-aware generation (Genarris), Z'>1 and multi-component handling, and why niching matters: the search must populate the correct low-energy region before any ranking method can succeed. The counterintuitive dip in success on the smallest molecules is a reminder that ranking-energy accuracy, not just sampling, decides blind-test wins -- motivating MLIP pre-screening plus high-level DFT and, where polymorphs sit within a few kJ/mol, finite-temperature free-energy corrections.
